I decided to keep 110 of the 125 affected people employed by moving them into plant roles that the Company otherwise fills by hiring from outside, and to offer severance to the remaining 15.

The main reason is value. Retraining costs $15,000 a person and pays back within two years compared with external hiring, and the plants need roughly 500 hires a year. Moving people internally therefore keeps experienced staff in work, reduces the disruption of a layoff for the community, and avoids the cost of recruiting and training outsiders. It also serves customers, who keep the same skilled workforce.

I chose the plant-pay path for most people (85). It has a one-time cost and no ongoing pay gap for the Company, which protects shareholder returns and the cash that can fund other stakeholders over twenty years. Its drawback is a sharp pay cut for business and financial operations staff (39.8%), so I did not put everyone on it.

I used the keep-current-pay path for 25 people, mainly business and financial operations staff facing the largest cut. Its cost is $16,560 a person a year, about $0.4 million a year for this group, which is affordable from existing cash and cushions the hardest impact. I kept it to a minority because, compounded over twenty years, it would become a large drain.

I eliminated 15 roles with severance. Severance is modest (about $8,902 a person), and it gives those who prefer to leave or cannot take the plant-role pay a clean exit. I did not use elimination more heavily, because removing people from work the community depends on, when internal openings exist, would weigh against the stakeholders I am meant to serve.

Cash after these paths remains above the minimum operating level, so the plan is fully funded. Overall, the mix balances employee security, Company economics, and the long-term interests of customers, suppliers, communities and shareholders.

Moving them into those roles preserves jobs and avoids outside hiring costs, and the $15,000 retraining cost pays back within two years.

I allocated 60 people to retraining into plant roles at plant pay. For most office and administrative support staff the pay change is small (about 1.5%), so this path is reasonable for them, and it is the lowest-cost way to keep people employed.

I allocated 40 people to retraining with current pay protected. Business and financial operations employees would face a 39.8% pay cut on the plant-pay path, which is a severe hardship. Protecting their pay costs about $16,560 a year per person, roughly $0.66 million a year for these 40, a recurring cost I judge acceptable given the employee and community impact over twenty years and the cash available.

I allocated 25 people to elimination with severance, about $0.2 million in total. This leaves a modest group who may prefer or be better served by a clean exit, and it limits the recurring pay differential and retraining spend. Retraining and keep-pay costs total roughly $6.8 million up front plus the recurring differential, all within the $44.1 million of cash above the minimum operating level.

The savings of $11.4 million a year are realized on every path. Customers, employees, and the communities the plants serve benefit from continued employment and skills development, while shareholders bear a modest, bounded cost. I will monitor retention, the pay differential, and plant staffing against the 500 annual hires to confirm the choice holds up.

I decided that none of the 125 people should lose their jobs, and that all of them should be retrained into plant roles that the Company otherwise fills by hiring from outside about 500 people a year.

The work in these two functions is no longer needed, so the $11.4 million a year saving is captured on every path. Elimination would be cheapest in the short term ($1.1 million of severance), but it ends income for people whose roles the Company can use, and it gives up a retraining payback of about two years against outside hiring. Eliminating people would also weigh heavily on employees and the communities around the plants, which the board's objective asks me to consider over twenty years.

I split the group by how much each would lose under the plant-pay path. Office and administrative support staff would lose only $839 a year (1.5%), so 70 of them move at plant pay. That keeps the Company's cost low, and the pay change is small. Business and financial operations staff would lose $36,569 a year (39.8%), a severe permanent cut, so the 55 of them keep current pay. The Company pays a top-up of $16,560 a person a year, about $0.9 million a year for this group, which is a real but bounded recurring cost against a large loss to employees.

The shareholder cost is recurring top-up pay, which I judge acceptable against the protection of employees' livelihoods. I will track the top-up cost and revisit the mix as the plant roles settle.
